messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos still remembers the sound of shattering glass and the screams that followed. It was a routine traffic stop gone wrong; he had been driving home from a late-night meeting with a client when police officers approached his car, guns drawn. The next thing he knew, he was being dragged out of the vehicle and thrown to the ground. A kick to the ribs left him gasping for air as he watched in horror as one of the officers slammed his head into the pavement. The memories of that night still haunt Carlos. Visible injuries or wounds on others now trigger a wave of anxiety; he can't help but think of his own battered body, the blood streaming down his face, and the feeling of utter powerlessness. Reminders of victims - news reports, conversations with friends who have had similar experiences - bring it all flooding back. Even physical pain in a part of his body, like the lingering ache in his ribs, can transport him back to that night. As he navigates his daily routine as a tax consultant, Carlos finds himself increasingly isolated and set apart from others. He feels like there's something about him that made the event happen - maybe it was his Latin American heritage, or perhaps it was just bad luck. Whatever the reason, he can't shake the feeling that he's to blame. His clients seem oblivious to his struggles, but Carlos is convinced they can see right through him, that they know he's not worth their time. Avoiding unfamiliar places has become second nature for Carlos; he sticks to routes he knows like the back of his hand, always on high alert for potential dangers lurking around every corner. He frequently looks over his shoulder, half-expecting to see a police officer or someone else with malicious intentions following him. Even in his own office, he identifies escape routes before feeling comfortable - just in case. The weight of these constant threat assessments has taken its toll on Carlos's mental health. He's started questioning whether his life is worth living anymore; the isolation and feelings of intrinsic fault have convinced him that he's a burden to those around him. His negative appraisals, in turn, fuel his hypervigilance - if he's not constantly on guard, he's sure something terrible will happen. As Carlos navigates this self-reinforcing cycle, he finds himself increasingly trapped. Triggers like visible injuries or victim memories send him spiraling back into the abyss of negative appraisals and threat assessments. It's a vicious loop that has finally brought him to seek help - not because he hopes to break free from it entirely, but because he fears what might happen if he doesn't. Carlos's eyes scan the therapist's office as he settles onto the couch, his gaze lingering on potential escape routes before returning to the present moment. He takes a deep breath and begins to recount his story, the words spilling out in a rush of anxiety and despair. As he speaks, it becomes clear that this is just the beginning - the first tentative step towards untangling the complex web of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals that has come to define his life.
